<reason>Both sides argued with unusual technical sophistication for this format, but B built the more robust core case: waste persists because destruction is structurally cheaper than coordination, so voluntary incentives sit "beside an open dumpster" and lose — a mechanism A never really rebutted beyond asserting incentives would work "in the overwhelming majority of cases." A's best weapon, the ex-ante ordering/newsvendor-style scarcity argument (managers can't distinguish future-surplus from future-sold stock, so they shave orders across the board), was clever and under-addressed by B's somewhat hand-wavy "two streams stay distinct" reply, but it remained speculative and unquantified, and real-world donation mandates elsewhere haven't obviously produced the shelf-emptying A predicts. B also landed a clean symmetry point on verification ("the paperwork didn't change, only the permission to refuse did") that A's closing answered only by re-assertion rather than fresh reasoning. Both sides handled Pressure Questions and A1/A2 format correctly, but B's closing converted A's own concession ("yes, a store stays free to trash food") into the debate's most memorable indictment, giving readers a cleaner single reason to vote PRO than CON's more diffuse implementation-cost narrative.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's pressure question "is a store still legally free to trash lawful edible food whenever the dumpster is cheaper?" and A's honest "Yes" answer, which B then converted in closing into "that is not flexibility, it is a license to destroy" — the single clearest crystallization of the whole clash.</best_rebuttal>
